content: Healthcare providers may harbor concerns about potential recrimination if community members are involved in the review processes. However, nearly all quality improvement frameworks emphasize the inclusion of community or user perspectives as a fundamental component. In the context of maternity services, the perspectives of women and the community are critical in defining what constitutes a high-quality service. This approach aligns with the broader goal of enhancing accountability within healthcare systems. As highlighted in Recommendation 10, involving communities in analyzing information and identifying solutions can enable healthcare services to better address the needs of the community. Community members can contribute to quality reviews either as informants or through discussions about healthcare information to identify ways to improve services. This can include consultations with communities, representation of community members on health facility management committees, and meetings between community representatives, service managers, and providers. The World Health Organization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of preventing and eliminating disrespect and abuse during facility-based childbirth. Evidence from studies conducted in lowand middle-income countries has identified facilitators and barriers to facility-based delivery. These studies suggest that community participation in quality improvement processes for maternity care services can be effective in increasing the use of skilled birth attendants and institutional births, as well as improving maternal and newborn health outcomes. Community participation in quality improvement processes is recommended to enhance the quality of care from the perspectives of women, communities, and healthcare providers. Communities should be actively involved in jointly defining and assessing quality. Mechanisms to ensure that women’s voices are meaningfully included are also strongly recommended, although the evidence supporting these recommendations is of low quality, and further research is needed. Evidence on interventions to involve communities in quality improvement processes was derived from systematic reviews. Participation processes and mechanisms varied across studies, and there was insufficient evidence to determine which strategies or combinations of strategies were most effective. Some studies reported positive effects of community participation, but the evidence was often weak and inconsistent. For example, one cluster randomized controlled trial in Uganda reported a significant increase in facility births, while other observational studies also noted increases in facility births following community participation interventions. For outcomes such as antenatal care (ANC) attendance, the evidence ranged from very low to moderate quality. Some studies reported increases in ANC visits, but the differences between intervention and control groups were not always significant. Similarly, for postpartum care, the evidence was rated as very low quality, with some studies showing increased coverage of postpartum care within 72 hours of birth following interventions. Community participation in quality improvement can take various forms, such as participation in stakeholder quality improvement committees or facilitated dialogue sessions involving representatives from both the community and health services. Key lessons include the importance of collaboration between community members and service providers to jointly define and improve quality, ensuring that pregnant women have a voice, and maintaining diversity in perspectives. Quality improvement committees can be effective when roles and responsibilities are clearly defined, and governance practices support participation. Ongoing monitoring of data is essential to inform the adaptation of strategies for continuous improvement and accountability. Health facility leadership that supports collaboration with communities is critical for the success of these approaches. Building trust among stakeholders and developing the capacity for joint planning and decision-making takes time. Data must be presented in accessible ways to ensure that all participants, regardless of their education or experience, can understand and engage with the information. While non-governmental organizations (NGOs) may have expertise in facilitating community involvement, their efforts should be linked to government services and embedded in ongoing processes. It is also important to include voices from diverse groups within the community to ensure equitable representation. Research gaps remain, including the dynamics of community-service interfaces in different settings, the processes of community and provider action planning, and the role of evolving technologies in supporting community participation. Additionally, mechanisms for community feedback on services and for providers to offer feedback to communities need further exploration. Advocacy efforts to improve service quality and the impact of participation on community dynamics, self-efficacy, and power relations also warrant further investigation.
